title: Global Scaling Effects and Long‐Term Disruptions by Invasive Ants
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

Biological invasions negatively impact biodiversity and ecosystem functions worldwide. Understanding the spatiotemporal dynamics of these impacts is crucial for improving management actions, yet how their impacts scale through space and time remains poorly resolved. Here, we synthesized effects of invasive ants and assessed how they vary geographically, and across ecological levels and invasion histories.

Location

Global.

Time Period

Studies included in meta-analysis were conducted between 1982 and 2023. The first recorded occurrences of invasive species in the study areas ranged from 1879 to 2018.

Major Taxa Studied

Ant species.

Methods

We conducted a global meta-analysis integrating 1817 effect sizes from 204 publications to assess ecological impacts caused by invasive ants. We evaluated the variation in effect sizes in trophic levels (from primary producer to predators and omnivores), ecological organization scale (from individual and population to community and ecosystem) and the geographical characteristics of invaded areas (i.e., insularity, habitat type and latitude).

Results

We found that invasive ants caused substantial changes in native species behaviour and abundance, community structure and ecosystem functions. We detected overall greater negative effects at higher levels of ecological complexity, with lasting negative effects for more than 60 years of residence time of invasive ants. Invasive ants caused rapid and persistent negative effects at lower levels of ecological organization (e.g., individual or population), while at higher levels (e.g., ecosystem) they manifested with a time lag of approximately 30 years. Finally, our systematic review identified only a small number of studies assessing impacts of invasive ants on ecosystem functions, in particular for 60 years or more of residence time, indicating important knowledge gaps.

Main Conclusions

This meta-analysis reveals that negative impacts caused by invasive species are greater at higher levels of ecological complexity in general, and that they tend to persist over one century and may accumulate at higher ecological levels over time.
